analysis.one_liner: Forces large meatpackers to buy a set share of cattle through open, negotiated markets and publish their contract terms publicly.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee on the day it was introduced, February 2, 2023, and stayed there until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: A handful of big companies buy most of the cattle slaughtered in the U.S., and most of those purchases happen under private formula contracts rather than open bidding, which many ranchers say lets packers suppress the price they pay. This bill, led by Senator Deb Fischer with a bipartisan group of 22 cosponsors, would have required USDA to publish a public library of the contracts packers use, and to set regional minimum percentages of cattle that large packers must buy through open negotiated markets, with fines up to $90,000 per weekly violation. It would also have sped up price reporting and required a study of alternative pricing methods. The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent cattle ranchers and feeders — the small and mid-size producers who sell to the big packers — would gain the most. They would be able to see, in a public library, the terms, premiums, and discounts packers actually offer, and they would benefit from minimum shares of cattle being bought through open negotiated bidding, which sets the market price everyone is paid against. Consumers could ultimately benefit if more competitive bidding lowers the packer margin built into retail beef prices.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a public library of the contracts packers use to buy cattle, including premium and discount schedules, so a producer can see what terms are available before negotiating.
Requires large packers to buy a minimum share of cattle through open, negotiated markets in each region — the trades that set the market price everyone else is paid against.

Speeds up price reporting: packers must report upcoming slaughter deliveries on a 14-day basis with prior-day submission, and USDA must publish expedited daily carcass-weight data and annual cutout-yield data.
Adds real penalties: up to $90,000 per weekly violation (adjusted for inflation) for packers that fail to meet the negotiated-trade minimums or refuse to file accurate contract information.

analysis.who_pays: The largest meatpacking companies — those slaughtering 5% or more of the nation's fed cattle — would bear the cost: they would have to disclose contract terms, buy a minimum percentage of cattle through open negotiated markets at each plant, and face fines up to $90,000 per weekly violation. Some of that cost, and some loss of contracting flexibility, could eventually show up in beef prices.

drawbacks.text: The mandatory minimum forces large packers to buy a set share of cattle through cash-style negotiated markets, which raises their costs and reduces their flexibility to lock in supply through long-term formula contracts — costs that could eventually show up in beef prices for consumers.

The bill puts heavy discretion in USDA: the department would draw the regions and set each minimum percentage (capped at 50%) through rulemaking, so the actual strength of the mandate would depend entirely on how the agency of the day writes the rules.

Opponents in the meatpacking and beef-processing industry have generally argued that mandated negotiated-trade percentages interfere with efficient markets and long-term supply arrangements, and that transparency alone does not fix thin negotiated markets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — knowing what cattle are actually worth before selling — would go to the independent ranchers and feeders who today sign contracts blind, and stronger price discovery would also give shoppers some protection against concentrated meatpacking margins. The costs are modest and administrative: packers would file contract details (with confidentiality protections intact), USDA would run the library, regions, and enforcement, and some processing decisions would carry a compliance burden. The mandatory minimum is the most debatable piece — it substitutes a government-set quota for market negotiation, and an honest supporter would concede that a one-size region mandate could interact poorly with local conditions even after a cost-benefit review. The transparency half alone is low-cost and broadly beneficial; the mandate half trades some market flexibility for more competitive bidding.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 2, 2023, with 22 cosponsors split evenly between Republicans and Democrats.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee.
No further action was ever recorded: the committee held no markup, the Senate never debated it, and it died at the end of the 118th Congress in January 2025 without a single vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The four large meatpackers who dominate cattle buying are better off: no contract library, no negotiated-trade minimums, and no fines were ever enacted.

for.name: Sen. Deb Fischer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 21 cosponsors.

for.name: Sens. Grassley, Tester, Wyden, Ernst, Braun and 17 other cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill even bipartisan support.

against.name: Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill in the two years after it was referred, letting it die without action.

against.name: Large meatpacking companies (JBS, Tyson, Cargill, National Beef)
against.what_they_did: The major beef packers opposed mandatory negotiated-trade minimums, which would have required them to buy a set share of cattle in open markets and exposed their contract terms publicly.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was evenly bipartisan — 11 of the Senate's 49 Republicans and 11 of the 48 Democrats signed on, led by a Republican — and the bill never became a partisan fight because it never advanced.

industries.industry: Large meatpacking companies (covered packers slaughtering 5%+ of fed cattle)
industries.note: They would have to disclose contract terms and premium schedules to a public library, buy a set share of cattle through open negotiated markets, and face fines up to $90,000 per weekly violation. Their pricing leverage over ranchers would shrink.

The bill's main beneficiaries: they would see the contract terms being offered market-wide and would sell more cattle into open negotiated markets where multiple buyers bid, rather than accepting a formula price set by one packer.
More competitive bidding at the ranch level could put downward pressure on the packer margin embedded in retail beef prices, though the bill could also add costs that pass through to shoppers.

They fall below the 5% national slaughter threshold and would not be covered packers, but more transparent pricing and livelier negotiated markets would generally improve the terms on which they buy cattle too.
